hero.title: Kolabr vs Slack
hero.lede: Both give your team channels and chat. The difference starts with the second channel you put a client in: in Slack that person becomes a billable seat, and in Kolabr they stay free. This page sets the two side by side on guest cost, request tracking, knowledge and price.

summary.title: The short version
summary.body: Kolabr does everything you use Slack for, then adds the parts you currently bolt on: requests with owners and deadlines, a wiki in every channel, and scheduled events. Guests are free wherever you put them, so you stop rationing who gets invited.

summary.title: Proof takes one week
summary.body: Give your most demanding client a channel and invite their whole team, not just one contact. By Friday the questions arrive from the people who actually have them, and every promise has an owner and a date against it.

statement.title: The second channel is where it gets expensive
paragraphs: Slack gives you free guests on one condition: one channel each, and no more than five for every paid member. It holds up while a client only ever needs a single room. It stops holding up the moment the same client has a project channel, a billing question and a support thread, because that person is now a multi-channel guest and is charged at your full seat rate.

Kolabr has one kind of guest. Free, in as many channels as the work requires, with no allowance to track and nothing that converts them into a paid seat later. The practical result is that you stop deciding who is worth inviting, and the people with the answers are simply in the room.

items.title: Are Slack guests free?
items.body: A single-channel guest is free, and you may have up to five of them for every paid active member. The moment that person needs a second channel they become a multi-channel guest and are billed at your full per-seat rate. So the honest answer is that guests are free while one channel is genuinely enough. In Kolabr a guest is free in any number of channels, with no allowance to count and no upgrade to trip over.

items.title: What is the difference between Slack Connect and a guest?
items.body: Slack Connect links a channel between two Slack workspaces, so each person stays in their own account under their own policies. It works well, with one condition: both organisations need a paid Slack plan. A client who does not use Slack, or uses the free plan, falls back to being a guest in your workspace. Kolabr has no equivalent condition, because a guest only needs an email address.

items.title: Is Kolabr cheaper than Slack?
items.body: Per internal seat the two are in the same territory once you compare like for like. The difference is everyone who is not staff. If you work with clients who need more than one channel, those people are billable seats in Slack and cost nothing in Kolabr, which is where the gap opens for agencies, firms and providers with a long client list.

items.title: Can Kolabr replace Slack entirely?
items.body: Yes, and most customers end up there. Kolabr runs internal team channels, private and group messages, calls and file sharing the same way it runs client channels. What it adds is the layer Slack leaves to other products: requests with owners and deadlines, a wiki in each channel, and scheduled events tied to the work they belong to.

items.title: What does Kolabr do that Slack does not?
items.body: Requests with a category, an owner and a response-time target the client can see. A wiki that lives in the channel and stays readable to guests. Scheduled events tied to the request that caused them. And unlimited free guests, which changes how many people you are willing to invite into the room.

items.title: We already have years of history in Slack. What happens to it?
items.body: Export it and keep it. Kolabr does not require you to move history to start, because the usual first step is a single client channel running alongside what you already have. Most teams find the archive matters less than they expected once the current work has one home.

hero.title: Kolabr vs Microsoft Teams
hero.lede: Teams was built for the people inside your company. Kolabr runs your internal channels too, and every client, contractor, consultant and supplier in the same place, on the same terms, without a second tool or a second bill. This page sets the two side by side on the things that decide it: what an outsider costs you, how quickly you can get them into a room, and whether anyone can tell what was promised.

summary.title: The short version
summary.body: Kolabr handles the internal room as readily as the client one: your own team channels, your own private and group chats. The difference shows the moment someone outside the company has to be in the conversation, which in most businesses is most days. Kolabr makes it easy and frictionless.

summary.title: Proof takes one week
summary.body: Give your most demanding client a channel and invite them. By Friday you will see it: they answer in the channel instead of the phone, every promise has an owner and a date, and nobody has asked you to resend anything. That is the week that decides it.

statement.title: The difference is what happens when someone is not on your payroll
paragraphs: In Teams, there are three different ways to bring in someone from outside, and you have to pick one before you start. One lets you chat to them but nothing more. One adds them to a team and creates an account for them in your company directory. One links your organisation to theirs, if their IT agrees to set it up too. Each is configured in a different place, and each has its own rules about what the person can see.

In Kolabr there is one mechanism. You invite an email address into a channel and that person is a member of that channel: able to read the wiki, raise a request, join a call, see the dates. They are never billed, they never appear in a directory you have to govern, and they cannot see any channel they were not invited to. That is the whole model, and it is why a firm with eleven staff can run two hundred client relationships without an administrator.

items.title: Can Microsoft Teams work with clients outside my company?
items.body: Yes. Microsoft offers three routes: external access (federation) for chat and calls with people in other Microsoft 365 domains, guest access to add someone into a team properly, and shared channels built on B2B direct connect. Each has a different security model and a different place to configure it, so the practical question is less whether it can and more how much administration stands between you and the first invitation. In Kolabr that step is an email address.

items.title: Do Microsoft Teams guests need a licence?
items.body: Not an extra Microsoft 365 licence. A guest does become a real identity in your directory, covered by Microsoft Entra External ID and its billing model, and counted in your tenant’s governance and access reviews. In Kolabr a guest is simply a person in a channel, never billed, never in a directory, and nothing to review later.

items.title: Is Kolabr cheaper than Microsoft Teams?
items.body: It depends on how many outside people you work with. Teams is priced per internal seat from $4, Kolabr from $9.99, but Kolabr never charges for a guest and needs nothing underneath it, so a ten-person firm working with two hundred clients pays for ten people. Once you add Teams Phone, Teams Premium or Copilot, the per-seat gap narrows or reverses. And if you already hold Microsoft 365 for mail and Office, cost is not the question worth asking: external collaboration is.

items.title: Can we use Kolabr and Microsoft Teams together?
items.body: Many do at first, and some stay that way. The usual path is to start with one client channel in Kolabr while Teams keeps whatever is wired into Office, SharePoint and Exchange, then move internal channels across as people ask for them, since Kolabr handles those too. Calendar sync means scheduled events land in Outlook throughout, so nobody ends up with two diaries.

items.title: What does Kolabr do that Teams does not?
items.body: Three things principally. Requests with a category, an owner and a response-time target, visible to the client. A wiki that sits beside the conversation in the same channel and that guests can read. And a channel boundary that means a client sees one channel and nothing else, without a tenant-level configuration exercise first.

items.title: Which one should we choose?
items.body: Ask which conversations currently go wrong. Kolabr runs your internal channels and your client channels in one place, with guests who are free and instant, requests carrying owners and deadlines, and a wiki beside the work. Teams is the stronger fit if what you mainly need is telephony and an AI layer across your mailbox. For most firms whose work involves people outside the company, the daily friction is the part Kolabr is built to remove.

hero.title: Kolabr vs Basecamp
hero.lede: Basecamp organises work into projects. Kolabr organises it around the people you work with, in a channel that does not end when one job does. Both let you bring clients in for free, so the real comparison is what happens to the relationship after the project closes, and whether anyone can tell what was promised while it was open.

summary.title: The short version
summary.body: A project ends. A client does not. Kolabr gives each relationship one channel that holds every request, every document and every conversation you have ever had with them, instead of an archive of finished projects you have to search through.

summary.title: Proof takes one week
summary.body: Take your longest-standing client, the one whose work never really stops, and give them a channel. By Friday you will have the whole relationship in one place, with every open item owned and dated.

statement.title: Most work does not have an end date
paragraphs: A project-shaped tool works beautifully for a thing with a beginning and an end: a launch, a build, a move. It starts to strain when the work is a relationship. A client you have had for six years is not a project. Neither is support, a retainer, a maintenance contract or a site you look after. Those produce a new project every few months and split the history across all of them.

A Kolabr channel is the relationship itself. The client joins once and stays. Work arrives inside it as requests, closes, and is still findable in two years alongside the wiki article that explains how you handled it. Nobody is re-invited, and nothing is archived away from the conversation that produced it.

sections.title: Tasks live inside the request, and die with it
paragraphs: Kolabr has tasks. What it does not have is a task manager. Every task belongs to the request that created it, is assigned to somebody, and disappears when that request is closed. There is no separate list to groom, no board that slowly fills with items nobody remembers agreeing to, and no second place to look for what is outstanding.

This is a deliberate limit. Free-standing to-do lists are easy to create and almost impossible to keep honest, and after a year they describe a version of the work that stopped being true months ago. Tying every task to a request means the list is always as current as the request it belongs to, and closing the request closes the loop.

hero.title: Kolabr vs Notion
hero.lede: Notion is where teams keep what they know. The conversation about it happens in a different tool, and the promise made to a client during that conversation happens in a third. Kolabr puts all three in one channel: the discussion, the request with an owner and a deadline, and the article that explains how you handle it.

summary.title: The short version
summary.body: A page cannot tell you what was promised or who owes it. Kolabr gives every client a channel where the conversation produces numbered requests with owners and deadlines, and the wiki sits right beside them.

summary.title: Proof takes one week
summary.body: Pick a client and open a channel. There is nothing to design first, no database to model and no template to choose. By Friday the conversation, the open requests and the wiki are in one place.

statement.title: The document is never where the conversation is
paragraphs: A decision gets made in chat. It is written up on a page somewhere else. The client is told by email, and the thing they asked for in return is remembered by one person. Three tools, three records, and no single answer to what is outstanding. This is the ordinary shape of a week for most teams, and it is not a Notion problem so much as the cost of splitting work across products that do not know about each other.

In Kolabr a channel holds the conversation, the requests it produced and the wiki that explains them. The client is in it. When somebody asks what was agreed, the answer is a request with a number, a date and a name, and the article beside it says how that kind of work is handled.

sections.title: A wiki small enough to stay true
paragraphs: Kolabr has a wiki in every channel, and it is deliberately not a company encyclopaedia. It holds what the people in that channel need: how a revision is issued, what counts as urgent, who signs what. Guests read it without a licence, and because its scope is one relationship it stays short enough that somebody actually maintains it.

The failure mode of a general knowledge tool is not that it cannot hold the information. It is that six hundred pages accumulate, nobody can tell which are current, and the honest answer to a question becomes asking a colleague instead. A wiki bound to one channel resists that, because its readers are the same handful of people every day.

sections.title: Tasks live inside the request, and die with it
paragraphs: Kolabr has tasks. What it does not have is a task manager. Every task belongs to the request that created it, is assigned to somebody, and disappears when that request is closed. There is no separate board to groom and no second place to look for what is outstanding, because what is outstanding for a client is the list of open requests.

This is a deliberate limit rather than a missing feature. Free-standing lists are easy to create and hard to keep honest, and a year in they describe a version of the work that stopped being true months ago. Tying every task to a request means the list is exactly as current as the request it belongs to.

hero.title: Kolabr vs Zendesk
hero.lede: A helpdesk is built for volume from people you will never meet. Kolabr is built for the forty clients whose names you know, where the request is one moment in a relationship that has run for years. Same discipline of owners, categories and clocks, without a portal standing between you and the person asking.

summary.title: The short version
summary.body: If your customers are strangers and there are thousands of them, buy a helpdesk. If they are named accounts you will still have in five years, the queue is the wrong shape and a channel is the right one.

summary.title: Proof takes one week
summary.body: Take one client off the portal and give them a channel. By Friday you will see requests arriving from people who never bothered to log in, and answers coming from colleagues who never had a seat.

statement.title: A queue is the wrong shape for forty named clients
paragraphs: Helpdesk software is designed around a stranger with a problem. It is why there is a portal, a form and a set of macros: when the volume is thousands a month from people you will never meet again, structure at the front door is what keeps it survivable. That design is a poor fit when the person raising the request is the same practice manager you spoke to yesterday and will speak to every week for the next three years.

In Kolabr the request sits inside the relationship rather than in front of it. The client is already in the channel, so they type, and one step turns that message into a numbered request with a category, an owner and a response target. The thread is attached, the history is right there, and nobody had to log in to a second system to tell you something.

items.body: No. Kolabr is priced per person on your plan, and anyone in your company can be in a channel and answer a request. Nobody has to decide whether a colleague is worth an agent seat before letting them help, and the client and their staff are guests at no cost.

items.title: Do clients need to log into a portal?
items.body: No. They are in the channel, which is where they already talk to you. There is no separate system to learn, no password to forget and no moment where somebody gives up and sends an email instead.

items.title: Can we run both?
items.body: Yes, and some do. A helpdesk handles high-volume inbound from the general public while Kolabr runs the named accounts, where the relationship matters more than the queue. The two rarely overlap in practice, because they are shaped for different kinds of customer.

items.title: What does Kolabr include that a helpdesk plan charges for?
items.body: A wiki in every channel instead of a help centre you build and publish, full chat with direct messages, video calls, and scheduled events. One price, with no per-agent add-ons stacked on it.

cta.title: Take one client off the portal.
cta.body: Fourteen days free on Max, every option included, no card. Keep the owners, categories and clocks; lose the front door.
